title: Prophets whose lives were worthy of the Spirit
source_text: Τῶν δ᾿ ἐν Ἰουδαίοις προφητῶν οἱ μὲν πρὸ τῆς προφητείας καὶ τῆς θείας κατακωχῆς ἦσαν σοφοὶ, οἱ δ᾿ ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς τῆς προφητείας φωτισθέντες τὸν νοῦν τοιοῦτοι γεγόνασιν, αἱρεθέντες ὑπὸ τῆς προνοίας εἰς τὸ πιστευθῆναι τὸ θεῖον πνεῦμα καὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ τούτου λόγους διὰ τὸ τοῦ βίου δυσμίμητον καὶ σφόδρα εὔτονον καὶ ἐλευθέριον καὶ πάντῃ πρὸς θάνατον καὶ κινδύνους ἀκατάπληκτον. τοιούτους γὰρ καὶ ὁ λόγος αἱρεῖ δεῖν εἶναι τοὺς τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεοῦ προφήτας. οἵτινες παίγνιον ἀπέφηναν τὴν Ἀντισθένους καὶ Κράτητος καὶ Διογένους εὐτονίαν. δι᾿ ἀλήθειαν γοῦν καὶ τὸ ἐλευθερίως ἐλέγχειν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας „ἐλιθάσθησαν, ἐπρίσθησαν, ἐπειράσθησαν, ἐν φόνῳ μαχαίρας ἀπέθανον· περιῆλθον γὰρ ἐν μηλωταῖς, ἐν αἰγείοις δέρμασιν, ὑστερούμενοι, κακουχούμενοι, ἐν ἐρημίαις πλανώμενοι καὶ ὄρεσι καὶ σπηλαίοις καὶ ταῖς ὀπαῖς τῆς γῆς, ὧν οὐκ ην ἄξιος ὁ ἐπὶ γῆς κόσμος“· ἀεὶ ἐνορῶντες τῷ θεῷ καὶ τοῖς ἀοράτοις τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ μὴ βλεπομένοις αἰσθητῶς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οὖσιν αἰωνίοις. ὁ δὲ βίος ἑκάστου τῶν προφητῶν ἀναγέγραπται· ἀρκεῖ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος παραθέσθαι τὸν Μωϋσέως βίον (καὶ γὰρ αὐτοῦ φέρονται προφητεῖαι, ἀναγεγραμμέναι ἐν τῷ νόμῳ) καὶ τὸν Ἱερεμἰου, φερόμενον ἐν τῇ ὁμωνύμῳ αὐτοῦ προφητείᾳ, καὶ τὸν Ἡσαΐου, ὃς ἐπορεύθη ὑπερτείνων πᾶσαν ἄσκησιν „γυμνὸς καὶ ἀνυπόδετος“ ἔτεσι τρισίν. ἴδε δὲ καὶ παιδαρίων, τοῦ Δανιὴλ καὶ τῶν σὺν αὐτῷ, τὸν ἐῤῥωμένον βίον, ἀναγνοὺς τὴν ὑδροποσίαν αὐτῶν καὶ ὅτι ἡ τροφὴ ἦν αὐτοῖς ὄσπριον, ἐμψύχων ἀπεχομένοις. εἰ δὲ δύνασαι, καὶ τὰ πρὸ τούτων θέασαι, Νῶε προφητεύσαντος καὶ Ἰσαὰκ τῷ υἱῷ ἐπευξαμένου προφητικῶς καὶ τοῦ Ἰακὼβ λέγοντος ἑκάστῳ τῶν δώδεκα· „δεῦτε, ἵνα ἀναγγείλω ὑμῖν, τί ἔσται ἐπ᾿ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν.“ οὗτοι δὴ καὶ ἄλλοι μυρίοι προφητεύσαντες τῷ θεῷ καὶ τὰ περὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ προεῖπον. διόπερ ἐν οὐδενὶ μὲν τιθέμεθα λόγῳ τὰ ὑπὸ τῆς Πυθίας ἢ Δωδωνίδων ἢ Κλαρίου ἢ ἐν Βραγχίδαις ἢ ἐν Ἄμμωνος ἢ ὑπὸ μυρίων ἄλλων λεγομένων θεοπρόπων προειρημένα· τὰ δ᾿ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ προφητευσάντων τεθήπαμεν, ὁρῶντες ὅτι ἄξιος ἦν αὐτῶν ὁ ἐῤῥωμένος καὶ εὔτονος καὶ σεμνὸς βίος πνεύματος θεοῦ, τρόπῳ προφητεύοντος καινῷ καὶ οὐδὲν ἔχοντι παραπλήσιον ταῖς ἀπὸ δαιμόνων μαντείαις.
pass_a_gloss: Of the prophets (προφήτης) among the Jews, some before the prophecy (προφητεία) and the divine possession (κατακωχή) were wise (σοφός); others, from the prophecy itself enlightened (φωτίζω) in mind (νοῦς), became such, having been chosen (αἱρέω) by providence (πρόνοια) to be entrusted (πιστεύω, passive) with the divine Spirit (πνεῦμα θεῖον) and the words (λόγος) from it, because of their life (βίος) being hard to imitate (δυσμίμητος), very vigorous (εὔτονος), free (ἐλευθέριος), and in every way undismayed (ἀκατάπληκτος) toward death and dangers. For reason (λόγος) also proves (αἱρέω) that such must be the prophets of the God over all (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός). Who showed up as a plaything (παίγνιον ἀποφαίνω) the vigour (εὐτονία) of Antisthenes, Crates and Diogenes. At least for truth (ἀλήθεια) and for freely (ἐλευθερίως) refuting (ἐλέγχω) those who sin [quotation]: 'they were stoned (λιθάζω), sawn (πρίζω), tempted (πειράζω), died in slaughter (φόνος) of sword; for they went about in sheepskins (μηλωτή), in goat skins, lacking (ὑστερέω), ill-treated (κακουχέω), wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth, of whom the world (κόσμος) on earth was not worthy (ἄξιος)'; always looking into (ἐνοράω) God and the invisible things (ἀόρατος) of God, not seen sensibly (αἰσθητῶς) and through this being eternal (αἰώνιος). The life of each prophet has been written up (ἀναγράφω); it suffices at present to set beside (παρατίθημι) the life of Moses (for his prophecies too are carried, written in the law, νόμος), and that of Jeremiah, carried in his namesake (ὁμώνυμος) prophecy, and that of Isaiah, who, exceeding (ὑπερτείνω) all discipline (ἄσκησις), walked 'naked and barefoot' (γυμνός, ἀνυπόδετος) three years. See also the robust (ῥώννυμι, perf. part.) life of the boys (παιδάριον), Daniel and those with him, having read their water-drinking (ὑδροποσία) and that their food (τροφή) was pulse (ὄσπριον), abstaining from animate things (ἔμψυχα). If you are able, view also those before these: Noah having prophesied, Isaac having prayed over (ἐπεύχομαι) his son prophetically, and Jacob saying to each of the twelve: 'come, that I may announce (ἀναγγέλλω) to you what will be at the last of the days.' These indeed and countless others, having prophesied for God, also foretold (προλέγω) the things about Jesus the Christ. Therefore we place in no account (λόγος) the things foretold by the Pythia or Dodonian women or the Clarian or at Branchidae or at Ammon's or by countless other so-called oracle-givers (θεοπρόπος); but those of the ones who prophesied in Judea we are astonished at (τέθηπα, perfect with present sense), seeing that their robust, vigorous and dignified (σεμνός) life was worthy of the Spirit of God, prophesying in a new (καινός) manner (τρόπος) and having nothing similar to the divinations (μαντεία) from demons (δαίμων).

lemmas.note: for his prophecies too are carried, written in the law

pass_b_english: Among the prophets of the Jews, some were wise before they received prophecy and divine possession; others became wise when their minds were enlightened by the prophecy itself. They were chosen by providence to be entrusted with the divine Spirit and the words that come from him because of their way of life: a life hard to imitate, exceedingly strenuous and free, and wholly undaunted in the face of death and danger. For reason, too, shows that the prophets of the God who is over all must be such men. They made the hardihood of Antisthenes, Crates and Diogenes look like a game. At any rate, for the sake of truth and for rebuking sinners freely, “they were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were tempted, they died by the sword; for they went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth, men of whom the world on earth was not worthy” (Hebrews 11:37–38). They always fixed their gaze on God and on the invisible things of God, which are not seen by the senses and are for that reason eternal (2 Corinthians 4:18).

The life of each of the prophets has been recorded. For the present it is enough to set before you the life of Moses (for prophecies of his, too, are handed down, written in the law); that of Jeremiah, related in the prophecy that bears his name; and that of Isaiah, who, going beyond every discipline, walked “naked and barefoot” for three years (Isaiah 20:2–3). Look also at the robust life of the boys, Daniel and his companions, when you have read that they drank water and that their food was pulse, since they abstained from living things (Daniel 1:12–16). And if you can, consider also what came before them: Noah, who prophesied (Genesis 9:25–27); Isaac, who prayed prophetically over his son (Genesis 27:27–29); and Jacob, who said to each of the twelve, “Come, that I may tell you what will happen in the last days” (Genesis 49:1). These men, and countless others who prophesied for God, also foretold what concerns Jesus the Christ.

That is why we hold in no account the things foretold by the Pythia, or the priestesses of Dodona, or the Clarian, or at Branchidae, or at the shrine of Ammon, or by countless other so-called oracle-givers. But what was prophesied by those in Judaea fills us with awe, for we see that their robust, strenuous and dignified life was worthy of the Spirit of God, who prophesies in a new way, nothing like the divinations that come from demons.

choices.choice: Origen’s own voice throughout; no words of Celsus are quoted in this chapter (the oracle list echoes Celsus’s list at 7.3). Hebrews 11:37–38 is quoted freely: Origen adds γάρ after περιῆλθον, omits θλιβόμενοι, moves ‘of whom the world was not worthy’ to the end, and reads ὁ ἐπὶ γῆς κόσμος (‘the world on earth’). ‘Not seen by the senses and therefore eternal’ alludes to 2 Corinthians 4:18; ‘the invisible things of God’ may also echo Romans 1:20 or Hebrews 11:27 (uncertain, not cited inline). Genesis 49:1 is quoted loosely: Origen has δεῦτε (‘come’) where the Septuagint reads συνάχθητε (‘gather together’), and τί ἔσται for τί ἀπαντήσει ὑμῖν. Noah’s prophecy (Genesis 9:25–27) and Isaac’s prophetic prayer over his son (Genesis 27:27–29, the blessing of Jacob; compare 27:39–40 for Esau) are identified by content, not wording. Daniel 1:12–16: the Greek Daniel has σπέρματα (‘seeds, pulse’); Origen paraphrases with ὄσπριον. ἐμψύχων ἀπεχομένοις rendered ‘abstained from living things’ (that is, from meat). ἀναγνούς is rendered ‘when you have read’, not as a second command. ἐλευθέριος (‘free, frank, noble’) is kept as ‘free’ to match ἐλευθερίως ἐλέγχειν (‘rebuking freely’) in the next sentence. παίγνιον ἀπέφηναν (‘made a plaything of’) rendered ‘made ... look like a game’. τεθήπαμεν rendered ‘fills us with awe’. Antisthenes, Crates and Diogenes are the Cynic philosophers, famed for endurance. The Moses, Jeremiah and Isaiah lives are general references to the books, not citations.
ἀναγνούς rendered as 'when you have read' instead of a second imperative 'read how'
ἐμψύχων ἀπεχομένοις: 'abstained from living things' (closer to the Greek than 'animal food')
τὰ πρὸ τούτων: 'what came before them' (neuter) instead of 'those who came before them'
'one that has nothing like' smoothed to 'nothing like'
Judea -> Judaea to match Book 7 chapter 3
Scripture checked: Hebrews 11:37–38, 2 Corinthians 4:18, Isaiah 20:2–3, Daniel 1:12–16, Genesis 9:25–27, 27:27–29, 49:1 all confirmed
